summary: A memo asking for reactions to a proposal to form an OS/2 user group. It is an informal request, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone asks, would anyone like to start a club for people who use this kind of computer system, and invites replies.

subtitle: Asking internet users: would you join an OS/2 user group?

tldr.problem: OS/2 individual users lacked a unified voice to communicate needs to IBM, unlike corporate IT organizations such as SHARE and GUIDE.
tldr.mechanism: The Phoenix Group, a founding council of ten OS/2 users, published this memo to gauge interest in forming a national OS/2 user group and solicited responses via email.
tldr.outcome: The RFC served as an informal poll to determine whether enough interest existed to approach IBM management about establishing a formal user advocacy organization.

today: RFC 1501 represents a grass-roots effort by OS/2 users to organize, reflecting the community-driven nature of early internet advocacy. OS/2 itself eventually declined in the market, though the RFC stands as a snapshot of user engagement in the early 1990s.

sections.title: The Need for a User Voice
sections.content: Corporate IT organizations like SHARE, GUIDE, and COMMON had long represented mainframe users to IBM, but individual OS/2 users had no equivalent organization. The RFC notes that users of Digital Equipment Company systems had DECIUS for representation, but OS/2 lacked a comparable advocacy group with a unified voice to influence IBM's product direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Big companies have clubs to talk to IBM, but regular people using OS/2 computers do not.

sections.title: The Founding Council
sections.content: The Phoenix Group consisted of ten long-time OS/2 users: Mike Andrews, Eric Brunsen, Max Eidswick, Robin Frank, Stan Hawkins, Jack Hiatt, Bob Holmes, Wayne Holmes, John Schaeffer, and Toby Pennycuff. They believed such an organization was an absolute necessity and were prepared to approach IBM's PSP (Personal Systems Products) senior management if sufficient interest existed.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of ten people who really like OS/2 started a project to create a user club.

sections.title: Measuring Interest
sections.content: The RFC asked recipients to send their name and address to either Z2934@AA1PROFS.IBMMAIL.COM or BRUNSENE@EMAIL.ENMU.EDU. The founders promised to compile a database of responses and keep respondents notified of progress electronically. The goal was to demonstrate to IBM that enough individual users wanted a unified organization that the company should support its creation.
sections.plainLanguage: The group asked people to say whether they wanted to join, and said they would tell everyone what happened.
